newsitem.title: USA: CBOT delivery changes face stiff opposition.
newsitem.headline: CBOT delivery changes face stiff opposition.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade's plan to change the delivery terms for its corn and soybean contracts has ignited a firestorm of opposition from scores of midwestern farmers, grain elevators and politicians.
More than 250 letters commenting on the proposal were sent to the Commodity Futures Exchange Commission as of Wednesday, according to a spokesman for the agency.

An overwhelming majority of letters opposed the CBOT plan to eliminate Toledo and St. Louis as delivery points for the contracts. The plan would also require that delivery be made through a shipping certificate instead of a warehouse receipt.
The corn and soybean contracts are used by farmers and agricultural businesses around the world to hedge their crops.

The CBOT, the world's largest futures market, was pressured by regulators late last year to make changes to the delivery terms of the two big contracts to reflect a sharp drop in Chicago grain storage space and changes in the cash grain market.
CFTC threatened to make its own recommendations if the exchange failed to come up with a solution.
But the response to the CBOT's plan was so negative that CFTC officials said privately they were considering reopening the public comment period for another two months.
Only a handful of letters, including submissions by Bunge Corp., Sen. Carol Mosely-Braun, R-Ill., and Continental Grain Co., expressed support for the CBOT's proposed changes.
Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar, R.-Ind., whose powerful committee oversees the agency's activities, urged regulators to listen to the complaints.
"Opposition to the new delivery system appears to be widespread among commercial users of these contracts," Lugar said in the April 10 letter. "I ask that you give careful study to these objections."
Two other U.S. senators -- John Glenn of Ohio and Mike DeWine of Ohio -- also told the CFTC they opposed the changes.
On Tuesday, members of the CBOT voted 423-to-211 to approve the controversial proposal.
But the proposal put forward by CBOT leaders found scant support among hedgers, grain elevators or other users of the exchange contracts.

The governors of Ohio and Michigan, the American Farm Bureau, Tyson Foods, the National Farmers Union, CSX Transportation, a local chapter of the International Longshoremen's Association and Canada's Ontario Soybean Growers wrote to the CFTC to urge the agency to reject the proposed changes.

Most said they opposed the changes because of the importance of keeping Toledo as a delivery point, the need to include a rail delivery option, and potential disruption of a 30-day shipping certificate for delivery, and the need to focus on the domestic market which accounts for the vast majority of soybean and corn usage.
